docs.title: Vision & Thesis
docs.text:
Long-term vision, not current capability

This page describes where SneppX-ALG is heading. It is not a description of what ships today. Capabilities such as per-inference integrity proofs and self-protecting execution are research goals; check Project scope and limitations and the security overview for what is implemented and tested now.

docs.title: Elevator Pitch
docs.text: SNEPPX-Algo is the first open-source AI algorithm with cryptographic integrity -- neuro-symbolic execution where every inference is verifiable, every execution path is tamper-proof, and the model evolves on-device without compromising privacy. The algorithm protects itself so you can run it anywhere without trusting the host.

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
Modern AI has a trust crisis:

  1. Closed models -- You don't know what the model is doing. You send data to an API and get back an answer. The computation is a black box.
  2. Open models can be tampered -- Even if the weights are public, nothing stops a malicious host from modifying the inference code, stealing the model, or poisoning the output.
  3. No verifiability -- There is no way to prove an inference was computed correctly without re-running it yourself.
  4. No on-device privacy -- Most "AI" requires sending your data to the cloud. On-device inference exists but lacks security guarantees.
  5. No open contribution model -- Open-source AI has no way to reward contributors or verify their contributions are honest.

docs.title: 1. Neuro-Symbolic Execution
docs.text: Combine neural network components (HSS, SER) with a symbolic program executor (NPE). The neural parts learn patterns; the symbolic parts verify logical correctness. The JIT pipeline optimizes hybrid programs at runtime.

docs.title: 2. Cryptographic Integrity
docs.text:
Every inference produces a zero-knowledge proof that it was computed correctly. Users verify the proof without re-running the model. This is mathematically-guaranteed trust.

  • Integrity proof: "This output is the correct result of model M on input X"
  • Privacy preserving: The proof reveals nothing about the model weights
  • Public verifiable: Anyone can check the proof with open-source verifier code

docs.title: 3. Self-Protecting Execution
docs.text:
The algorithm encrypts its own memory, obfuscates its control flow, detects debuggers, and virtualizes critical functions. Running SNEPPX on an untrusted host is safer than running any other model anywhere.

  • S0: All crypto primitives are constant-time, side-channel resistant
  • S1: All allocations have guard pages, canaries, ASLR
  • S2: Control flow is flattened, strings are encrypted, handlers are scrambled

docs.title: 4. On-Device First
docs.text:
The core algorithm is designed to run on phones and edge devices, not just datacenter GPUs.

  • Quantization-aware execution paths (INT8, FP8, AWQ, GPTQ)
  • Sparse compute (MoE routes to only a few experts per token)
  • Memory-efficient secure allocator (S1)
  • No cloud dependency for inference

docs.title: 5. Federated Contribution Protocol
docs.text:
Open-source AI needs an incentive and verification model. SNEPPX lets contributors train shards locally and submit cryptographically signed gradient contributions via the NCCL sync bridge. The protocol verifies contributions without seeing private data, turning the community into a distributed training network.

  • Gradient contributions are signed with Ed25519 (S0)
  • Contributions are aggregated via trust-weighted all-reduce (FM + NCCL)
  • Contributors earn reputation scores based on verification

docs.title: 6. Formal Safety Guarantees
docs.text: The behavioral monitor (S3) enforces provable constraints at runtime -- not just "detect anomalies" but "prove the output satisfies safety bounds." Combined with the symbolic execution layer, every decision path is auditable.

docs.title: Design Principles
docs.text:
1. Trust is mathematical, not organizational. Don't ask users to trust a company. Give them a proof.
  2. Security is foundational, not bolted on. Every layer from the allocator up is hardened.
  3. Open source is non-negotiable. The code, the proofs, the protocols -- all public.
  4. On-device is the default. Cloud is optional, not required.
  5. Contribute and verify. The community grows through cryptographically verified contributions.

docs.title: What Makes This Next-Gen
docs.text:
Most "next-gen AI" is just bigger models trained on more GPUs. SNEPPX-Algo is next-gen because it rethinks the relationship between the algorithm and the user:

  • From black box -> verifiable
  • From trust-the-company -> trust-the-math
  • From cloud-only -> on-device-first
  • From centralized training -> federated contribution
  • From reactive safety -> provable safety

This isn't a better transformer. It's a fundamentally different category of AI system.

docs.title: Autograd Guide
docs.text:
SneppX-ALG provides reverse-mode automatic differentiation and selected higher-order differentiation paths. Operator and backend coverage is still evolving; the presence of an API does not imply parity with PyTorch or a guarantee that every gradient path is validated.

See it happen

New to autograd? Start with the Autograd visualizer — type a scalar expression and watch gradients flow backwards through the graph.

docs.title: Basic usage
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from SneppX_ALG import Tensor

x = Tensor(np.array([2.0, 3.0]), requires_grad=True)
y = (x * x).sum()
y.backward()
print(x.grad)  # [4, 6]

docs.title: No-grad context
docs.text:
from SneppX_ALG.interface_bindings.autograd import no_grad

with no_grad():
    z = x * 2  # no graph built

docs.title: Higher-order AD (create_graph)
docs.text:
x = Tensor(np.array([1.0, 2.0]), requires_grad=True)
y = (x ** 2).sum()
y.backward(create_graph=True)
# x.grad now has a graph attached
g2 = (x.grad * x.grad).sum()
g2.backward()

docs.title: Forward-mode (jvp) and reverse-mode (vjp)
docs.text:
from SneppX_ALG.interface_bindings.autograd import jvp, vjp

def f(x):
    return (x * x).sum()

x = Tensor(np.array([1.0, 2.0, 3.0]), requires_grad=True)
tangent = Tensor(np.array([1.0, 1.0, 1.0]))
jvp_result = jvp(f, x, tangent)

docs.title: Gradient checkpointing
docs.text:
from SneppX_ALG.interface_bindings.grad_checkpoint import checkpoint

def heavy(x):
    return x * x

out = checkpoint(heavy, x)

docs.title: Higher-order differentiation coverage
docs.text:
Higher-order differentiation is implemented for a growing set of operations. Coverage differs by operation, dtype, and backend. Consult the current tests and the framework parity roadmap before relying on a specific higher-order gradient. Do not infer complete coverage from the existence of a class or function.

The jvp API is also under active correctness work; verify its behavior for your operation and backend before using it in a production numerical pipeline.

docs.title: Autograd visualizer
docs.text:
Type a scalar expression, then watch the forward values appear and the backward pass propagate gradients through the graph. No installation — this runs entirely in your browser.

▶ Run Step backward Reset Presets: (a*b+c)*relu(a) square(a)+exp(b) tanh(ab)/(1+c²) sqrt|w|·log(eˣ+1)

docs.title: How to read it
docs.text:
• Each box is a node: the operator on top, its forward value in the middle, and the gradient ∂f/∂node above it once the backward pass reaches it.
  • Edges point from inputs to their consumer, so the backward pass runs right-to-left.
  • relu has a subgradient of 0 for negative inputs — that's why a gradient can vanish at a node.

docs.title: How reverse-mode autodiff works
docs.text:
Automatic differentiation applies the chain rule to the graph above. The forward pass computes and stores each node's value. The backward pass starts at the output with gradient 1 and walks the graph in reverse. At each node it multiplies the incoming gradient by the node's local derivative and adds the result to each input's gradient.

Two details explain most of what you see in the visualizer:

  • Gradients add up. When a variable feeds several nodes, its gradient is the sum of the contributions from every path.
  • One backward pass gives every gradient. Reverse mode computes ∂f/∂x for all inputs at once, which is why it is the standard choice for training networks with millions of parameters and a single scalar loss.

SneppX-ALG's tensor engine uses the same tape-based approach and also supports higher-order gradients; see Higher-order AD.

docs.title: Supported syntax
docs.text:
Element Examples Variables a, b, c, x, w Arithmetic + - * / ** and unary - Functions relu, exp, log, sqrt, square, tanh, abs Grouping ( ... )

Everything is scalar-valued, so the graph stays small and readable. For the real tensor engine, see the Autograd guide and the Cookbook.

docs.title: 1. Prerequisites
docs.text:
Required:

  • CMake 3.16+
  • C11/C++20 compiler (MSVC 19.44+, GCC 11+, Clang 14+)
  • Python 3.9+ (for bindings)

Optional:

  • CUDA 12.0+ (GPU optimizer acceleration, SNEPPX_BUILD_CUDA=ON)
  • Doxygen (API docs)

docs.title: 2. Quick Build (All Targets)
docs.text:
This project is Ninja-based. Use the CMake presets (see CMakePresets.json), which select the Ninja generator and write to per-config binary directories.

Windows (MSVC):

git clone https://github.com/SneppX/sneppx-alg.git
cd sneppx-alg
cmake --preset release
cmake --build --preset release

Linux/Mac (GCC/Clang):

git clone https://github.com/SneppX/sneppx-alg.git
cd sneppx-alg
cmake --preset release
cmake --build --preset release -j$(nproc)

The release preset configures Release + LTO + tests; debug, asan, cuda, python, and minimal presets are also available.

docs.title: 3. Build Individual Targets
docs.text:
Build into the active binary directory (e.g. build/release after the release preset), then reference targets:

# Core kernel library
cmake --build build/release --config Release --target neural_core_kernel

# Architecture algorithms
cmake --build build/release --config Release --target neural_architecture_layer

# Security C library
cmake --build build/release --config Release --target neural_security_c

# Security C++ obfuscation
cmake --build build/release --config Release --target neural_security_cpp

# Python bindings
cmake --build build/release --config Release --target _SNEPPX_c

# CUDA kernels (requires CUDA SDK; use the `cuda` preset)
cmake --preset cuda
cmake --build --preset cuda --target neural_cuda_kernels

docs.title: 5. Debug Build
docs.text:
Use the debug preset (Ninja, Debug build type, tests+tools on):

cmake --preset debug
cmake --build --preset debug

Debug builds disable optimization and enable assertions. Use -DSNEPPX_S1_SECURE_MEMORY=OFF for faster debug iteration.

docs.title: 6. Python Package Build

pip install -e .

# With CUDA support
pip install -e .[cuda]

# Build wheel

docs.title: 7. Running Tests
docs.text:
Run from the binary directory of the active preset (e.g. build/release):

# C tests
cd build\release
ctest -C Release --output-on-failure

# Specific test
ctest -C Release -R test_kyber

# Sanitizer tests (Windows)
powershell -File scripts/run_sanitizers.ps1

For Python-only tests (no build required):

$env:PYTHONPATH = "bindings/python"
python -m pytest tests/python/ -v

docs.text: Issue Fix cuda_runtime.h: No such file or directory Build without CUDA: -DSNEPPX_BUILD_CUDA=OFF pybind11_add_module: Unknown CMake command Set pybind11_DIR or ensure FetchContent can reach GitHub LNK2001: unresolved external symbol Build neural_core_kernel and neural_security_c before _SNEPPX_c MSVC "no VLAs" Use calloc/free instead of stack-allocated VLAs __int128 undeclared on MSVC Guard with #ifndef NO_UINT128 (see x25519.c pattern) CreateProcess failed: The system cannot find the file specified. (MASM, Windows+Ninja) Use the stable Ninja 1.12+ (see scripts/ or repo root ninja.exe); the Kitware dev Ninja in the venv can crash. The x64 MASM path (ml64) is resolved automatically — no manual -DCMAKE_ASM_MASM_COMPILER needed.

docs.title: 9. Build Directories
docs.text:
The project standardizes on CMake presets (CMakePresets.json), each using the Ninja generator and writing to a per-config binary directory. Prefer the presets:

  • cmake --preset release → build/release
  • cmake --preset debug → build/debug
  • cmake --preset asan → build/asan
  • cmake --preset cuda → build/cuda
  • cmake --preset python → build/python
  • cmake --preset minimal → build/min

Avoid configuring the plain build/ directory with the presets; it is reserved for the legacy Visual Studio generator and is not Ninja-clean. See DEVELOPMENT.md for the full development workflow.

docs.title: Code Walkthrough — The SNEPPX-Alg Pipeline
docs.text: This is the entry point for reading the SNEPPX-Alg source. It maps the five pipeline stages to their directories, header APIs, and per-module walkthroughs.

docs.title: The five-stage pipeline
docs.text:
SNEPPX-Alg processes data through a fixed pipeline of five algorithm families. Each stage is a directory under algorithms/ and a public header under include/neural_core/architecture/.

Stage Name Header Directory Job 1 HSS — Hierarchical State Space hierarchical_state_space.h algorithms/hss/ Recurrent sequence modeling with a learnable state 2 SER — Sparse Expert Routing sparse_expert_routing.h algorithms/ser/ Mixture-of-experts gating, routing, and load balancing 3 ARC — Adversarial Robustness Certification adversarial_robustness_certification.h algorithms/arc/ Input guard, gradient obfuscation, output verification 4 NPE — Neural Programming Engine neural_programming_engine.h algorithms/npe/ 16-register neural VM with 32 opcodes and a JIT 5 FM — Fractal Memory Orchestrator fractal_memory_orchestrator.h algorithms/fm/ Distributed memory banks, sync, and federated state

The pipeline is HSS → SER → ARC → NPE → FM: sequence features are extracted, sparsely routed through experts, adversarially hardened, executed as a differentiable program, then written into distributed memory.

docs.title: Shared foundations
docs.text:
Every stage is built on three kernel subsystems (under include/neural_core/ and kernel/):

  • multidimensional_tensor_engine.h — the SNEPPXTensor core used by every stage as its data type.
  • automatic_differentiation_framework.h — the SNEPPXTape / SNEPPXVariable autodiff graph used for training.
  • polymorphic_memory_allocator.h — the memory allocator used for allocation in each module's C sources.

docs.title: How each module is organized
docs.text:
Every algorithm directory follows the same layout:

  • algorithms/<stage>/core/*.c — CPU implementation of the stage.
  • algorithms/<stage>/cuda/*.cu / *.cuh — CUDA kernels (built only when -DSNEPPX_BUILD_CUDA=ON).
  • include/neural_core/architecture/<stage>.h — the public API.

docs.title: Per-module walkthroughs
docs.text: Module Walkthrough HSS walkthrough-hss.md SER walkthrough-ser.md ARC walkthrough-arc.md NPE walkthrough-npe.md FM walkthrough-fm.md

docs.title: Recommended reading order
docs.text:
1. Start with walkthrough-hss.md — it introduces the tensor, layer, and train-graph patterns that the other four modules reuse.
  2. walkthrough-ser.md — adds gating and routing on top.
  3. walkthrough-arc.md — the security hardening stage.
  4. walkthrough-npe.md — a different execution model (a bytecode VM instead of plain tensor layers).
  5. walkthrough-fm.md — memory and distributed sync.

Each walkthrough ends with a "minimal example" that compiles against the library, and the full public API of the module.

docs.title: Coding conventions
docs.text:
• SNEPPX_ prefix for all public C functions, types, and macros

  • Python: Tensor.data is a COPY — rebuild perturbed tensors for FD checks

  • Additive-only: never rename/remove existing public items

docs.title: Conv2d visualizer
docs.text:
A convolution slides a small kernel over the input. Hover any output cell to see the exact window of input it read — and how stride and padding change the output size.

padded input ∗ kernel = output stride 1 padding 0 🎲 Randomize

docs.title: The output-size formula
docs.text:
out = floor((H + 2·pad − kernel) / stride) + 1

With H = 7, kernel = 3:

stride pad output 1 0 5×5 1 1 7×7 2 0 3×3 2 1 4×4

SNEPPX-Alg's nn.Conv2d supports stride, padding, dilation, and groups, and its backward pass is exact (verified against finite differences in tests/python/test_conv2d_autograd.py).

import numpy as np
from SneppX_ALG import Tensor
from SneppX_ALG.interface_bindings import nn

conv = nn.Conv2d(1, 4, kernel_size=3, stride=1, padding=1)
x = Tensor(np.random.randn(1, 1, 7, 7).astype(np.float32))
print(conv(x).shape)   # (1, 4, 7, 7)

docs.title: Output size formula
docs.text:
For an input of height H, kernel size K, padding P, stride S and dilation D, the output height is:

H_out = floor((H + 2·P − D·(K − 1) − 1) / S) + 1

The same formula applies to width. Two common settings are worth memorising:

  • K=3, P=1, S=1 keeps the spatial size unchanged ("same" padding).
  • S=2 roughly halves the spatial size, which is how many networks downsample without a separate pooling layer.

Each output channel has its own kernel that spans every input channel, so a Conv2d(C_in, C_out, K) layer holds C_out · C_in · K · K weights plus C_out biases.

See also: Matmul visualizer · Autograd visualizer.

docs.title: Cookbook — common recipes
docs.text: Small, copy-pasteable recipes. Every Python block has a ▶ Run button that executes it in your browser (Pyodide + SneppX-Alg), so you can experiment without installing anything.

docs.title: Freeze a layer (stop gradients)
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from SneppX_ALG.interface_bindings import nn

m = nn.Linear(4, 4)
for p in m.parameters():
    p.requires_grad_(False)
trainable = sum(p.numel for p in m.parameters() if p.requires_grad)
print("trainable elements:", trainable)

docs.title: Gradient clipping (global norm)
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from SneppX_ALG import Tensor
from SneppX_ALG.interface_bindings import nn, optim
from SneppX_ALG.interface_bindings.trainer_v2 import clip_grad_norm_

m = nn.Linear(4, 4)
opt = optim.Adam(m.parameters(), lr=1e-2)
x = Tensor(np.random.randn(8, 4).astype(np.float32))
y = Tensor(np.random.randn(8, 4).astype(np.float32))
loss = nn.functional.mse_loss(m(x), y)
loss.backward()
before = clip_grad_norm_(list(m.parameters()), max_norm=1.0)
print("total grad norm before clipping:", round(float(before), 4))

docs.title: Custom autograd Function
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from SneppX_ALG import Tensor
from SneppX_ALG.interface_bindings import autograd

class SquareFn(autograd.Function):
    @staticmethod
    def forward(ctx, x):
        ctx.save_for_backward(x=x)
        return Tensor(x.data ** 2, dtype=x.dtype)

    @staticmethod
    def backward(ctx, grad_output, create_graph=False):
        x = ctx.get_saved_tensor("x")
        return [Tensor(2 * x.data * grad_output.data, dtype=grad_output.dtype)]

x = Tensor(np.array([1.0, 2.0, 3.0], dtype=np.float32), requires_grad=True)
y = SquareFn.apply(x)
y.sum().backward()
print("forward:", y.data)
print("gradient:", np.asarray(x.grad.data))

docs.title: Learning-rate warmup + cosine decay
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from SneppX_ALG import Tensor
from SneppX_ALG.interface_bindings import nn, optim, schedulers

m = nn.Linear(4, 2)
opt = optim.Adam(m.parameters(), lr=0.01)
sched = schedulers.LinearWarmupCosineDecay(opt, total_steps=20, warmup_steps=5)

lrs = []
for step in range(8):
    x = Tensor(np.random.randn(8, 4).astype(np.float32))
    loss = m(x).sum()
    loss.backward()
    opt.step()
    opt.zero_grad()
    sched.step()
    lrs.append(round(float(opt.lr), 6))
print("lr schedule:", lrs)

docs.title: Reproducibility seed
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from SneppX_ALG import Tensor

np.random.seed(42)
a = Tensor(np.random.randn(3).astype(np.float32))

np.random.seed(42)
b = Tensor(np.random.randn(3).astype(np.float32))

print("reproducible:", np.allclose(a.data, b.data))

docs.title: Distributed Training
docs.text:
SneppX-ALG includes distributed-training API foundations and a deterministic DistributedSampler. Validated multi-process training is not available in the current Python backend. Process-group initialization, gradient collectives, FSDP sharding, and multi-node orchestration must not be treated as working features.

The Python API now fails explicitly when WORLD_SIZE is greater than one. This is intentional: a job that appears to train while gradients are not synchronized is worse than an explicit unsupported-operation error.

docs.title: What works today
docs.text:
• Single-process training with the ordinary tensor, module, optimizer, and trainer APIs.
  • DistributedSampler index partitioning when used as a local utility. It divides indices deterministically; it does not communicate between ranks.
  • Single-process calls to allreduce, allgather, and reduce_scatter return the input unchanged because there is only one participant.

docs.title: What is not supported
docs.text:
Capability Current status Multi-rank process-group initialization Unsupported; fails closed NCCL-backed Python collectives Not implemented in the Python adapter DDP gradient synchronization Unsupported for multiple ranks FSDP parameter/gradient sharding Experimental wrapper; multi-rank construction is rejected ZeRO stages 1–3 Not supported as end-to-end distributed training Pipeline, tensor, and expert parallelism Not validated end to end Elastic multi-node training Not supported

The presence of C/CUDA/NCCL source files or API names does not establish a working distributed runtime. A capability will be promoted to supported only after communicator setup, data movement, synchronization, error handling, and multi-process integration tests pass on the advertised hardware.

docs.title: Single-process example
docs.text:
from SneppX_ALG import Tensor
from SneppX_ALG.interface_bindings import nn, optim

model = nn.Linear(4, 2)
optimizer = optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3)

inputs = Tensor.randn((8, 4))
targets = Tensor.randn((8, 2))

predictions = model(inputs)
loss = nn.functional.mse_loss(predictions, targets)
optimizer.zero_grad()
loss.backward()
optimizer.step()

docs.title: Sampler utility example
docs.text:
from SneppX_ALG import DistributedSampler

dataset = list(range(10))
rank_zero_indices = list(
    DistributedSampler(dataset, num_replicas=2, rank=0, shuffle=False)
)
rank_one_indices = list(
    DistributedSampler(dataset, num_replicas=2, rank=1, shuffle=False)
)
assert rank_zero_indices == [0, 2, 4, 6, 8]
assert rank_one_indices == [1, 3, 5, 7, 9]

These index partitions are useful for testing input sharding logic locally, but they do not make a multi-rank training loop valid.

docs.title: Roadmap
docs.text: The implementation order is: establish a real process-group lifecycle, add validated CPU collectives, integrate NCCL communicator creation and unique-ID exchange, then test DDP gradient synchronization. FSDP/ZeRO and pipeline, tensor, and expert parallelism depend on those foundations.

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text: This guide walks you through installing SNEPPX-Alg and running your first training loop.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
pip install sneppx-alg

Or install in development mode from source:

git clone https://github.com/SneppX/sneppx-alg.git
cd sneppx-alg
pip install -e .

To run with local development bindings without installation:

$env:PYTHONPATH = "bindings/python"

docs.title: First Tensor & Autograd
docs.text:
Tensors support automatic differentiation out of the box with tape-based backpropagation:

import numpy as np
from SneppX_ALG import Tensor

# Create a tensor requiring gradients
x = Tensor(np.array([2.0, 3.0, 4.0], dtype=np.float32), requires_grad=True)

# Forward arithmetic
y = (x * x + 3.0 * x).sum()

# Backward pass to compute dy/dx
y.backward()

print("x.grad:", x.grad)  # [7.0, 9.0, 11.0]

docs.title: First Neural Network Training Loop
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from SneppX_ALG import Tensor, F
from SneppX_ALG.interface_bindings import nn, optim

np.random.seed(0)

class MLP(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.fc1 = nn.Linear(4, 8)
        self.fc2 = nn.Linear(8, 2)

    def forward(self, x):
        return self.fc2(F.relu(self.fc1(x)))

model = MLP()
opt = optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=1e-2)

for step in range(200):
    x = Tensor(np.random.randn(32, 4).astype(np.float32))
    y = Tensor((2.0 * x.data[:, :2]).astype(np.float32))

    loss = F.mse_loss(model(x), y)
    loss.backward()

    opt.step()
    opt.zero_grad()

print("final loss:", round(float(np.asarray(loss.data).reshape(-1)[0]), 4))

docs.title: Higher-Order Autodiff
docs.text: SNEPPX-Alg supports higher-order differentiation via create_graph=True.

docs.title: Computing Hessians
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from SneppX_ALG import Tensor

x = Tensor(np.array([1.0, 2.0, 3.0]), requires_grad=True)
y = (x ** 2).sum()
y.backward(create_graph=True)
# x.grad is now a tensor with a graph
hessian = (x.grad * x.grad).sum()
hessian.backward()

  • Quadratic forms

  • LayerNorm, RMSNorm
  • All loss functions

docs.title: HSS training guide
docs.text: This guide explains how to build, run, and train a Hierarchical State Space (HSS) model with SNEPPX-Alg, end to end, on CPU. It walks through the autodiff tape, the layer-normalization step, and a minimal training loop.

docs.title: 1. Model and parameters
docs.text:
An HSS model is created from a config and a seed:

SNEPPXHSSConfig cfg;
cfg.state_dim   = 4;
cfg.input_dim   = 4;
cfg.output_dim  = 4;
cfg.num_layers  = 1;
cfg.seq_len     = 1;
cfg.dt_min      = 0.01f;
cfg.dt_max      = 0.1f;
cfg.use_hierarchical = 0;

SNEPPXHSSModel* model = SNEPPX_hss_model_create(&cfg, 42);

Per-layer parameters (9 tensors each) are enumerated by SNEPPX_hss_get_params:

idx name meaning 0 A state transition 1 B input->state 2 C state->output 3 D feedthrough 4 dt per-step size 5 xp input projection weight 6 xpb input projection bias 7 ng layer-norm gain (norm_gamma) 8 nb layer-norm shift (norm_beta)

docs.title: 2. Building the training graph
docs.text:
Each training step:

  1. Wraps the model parameters in SNEPPXVariable* (with requires_grad = 1).
  2. Builds the forward graph with SNEPPX_hss_build_train_graph.
  3. Attaches an SNEPPX_mse_loss.
  4. Runs SNEPPX_tape_backward.
  5. Steps the optimizer (CPU or CUDA-accelerated).
  6. Destroys the tape (after nulling the weight data pointers).
SNEPPXTape* tape = SNEPPX_tape_create();

SNEPPXVariable** wv = /* SNEPPX_variable_create(pt[i], 1) for each param */;
SNEPPXVariable* inv = SNEPPX_variable_create(input, 0);

SNEPPXVariable* outv = NULL;
SNEPPX_hss_build_train_graph(model, tape, inv, wv, nw, &outv);

SNEPPXVariable* tgv  = SNEPPX_variable_create(target, 0);
SNEPPXVariable* loss = SNEPPX_mse_loss(tape, outv, tgv);

SNEPPX_tape_backward(tape, loss);

SNEPPXTensor** gt = /* wv[i]->grad */;
SNEPPX_optimizer_step(opt, pt, gt, nw);

docs.title: 3. The layer-norm step
docs.text:
Inside SNEPPX_hss_build_train_graph (file algorithms/hss/core/forward_train.c), each timestep computes:

x_col  -> xp_out = matmul(xp, xt_col)
       -> xp_b   = add(xp_out, xpb)
       -> xp_norm  = layer_norm(xp_b, ng, nb, 1e-5)     <- gain/shift here
       -> h_new  = add(matmul(A_bar, h), matmul(B_bar, xp_norm))
       ...

SNEPPX_layer_norm stores ctx->gamma = gamma (the variable). Its backward reads the float buffer as c->gamma->data->data (not c->gamma->data).

docs.title: 4. Optimizer
docs.text:
SNEPPXOptimizerConfig opt_cfg = SNEPPX_optimizer_config_default();
opt_cfg.learning_rate = 0.03f;
opt_cfg.type = SNEPPX_OPTIMIZER_ADAM;
SNEPPXOptimizer* opt = SNEPPX_optimizer_create(&opt_cfg);

// Optional: use CUDA-accelerated optimizer
SNEPPXTrainConfig train_cfg = SNEPPX_train_config_default();
train_cfg.use_cuda_optimizer = 1;  // requires SNEPPX_BUILD_CUDA=ON

SNEPPX_optimizer_step(opt, params, grads, n) applies the update in place. When use_cuda_optimizer=1, the trainer transparently transfers params/grads to GPU and runs cuBLAS SGD or AdamW.

docs.title: 5. Verifying training works
docs.text:
Run the bundled integration test:

cmake --preset release
cmake --build build --config Release --target test_train_integration
& build\tests\Release\test_train_integration.exe

Expected (v0.9.7):

init=0.234858 final=0.015788 ratio=0.0672
PASS

Loss should drop by >90% over 10 Adam steps.

docs.title: 6. Tips
docs.text:
• Learning rate: 0.03 with Adam over 10 steps is enough to show convergence.
  • Determinism: fixed seed + Adam => reproducible runs.
  • CUDA optimizer: Enable use_cuda_optimizer for GPU-accelerated optimizer steps. The forward and backward passes remain on CPU.
  • Don't free params via the tape: null wv[i]->data before SNEPPX_tape_destroy so the model's parameter tensors survive across steps.

docs.text:
Pick a loss function and see both its value and its gradient. The gradient is what the optimiser actually follows, so two losses that look similar can behave very differently in training.

loss

docs.title: Why the gradient matters more than the value
docs.text: Loss Gradient for large error Effect MSELoss grows linearly outliers dominate the update L1Loss constant robust to outliers, but noisy near zero HuberLoss clipped at δ quadratic near zero, linear in the tails SmoothL1Loss → sign(z) same idea, C¹-continuous at ±β log-cosh → ±1, smoothly robust and differentiable everywhere Geman-McClure → 0 bounded influence: very strong outlier rejection HingeLoss 0 once satisfied no gradient for already-correct margins BCEWithLogits → −1 never stops pushing on badly wrong predictions focal loss → 0 for easy examples down-weights well-classified samples quantile loss asymmetric pinball loss for a τ-quantile forecast

docs.title: Robust vs sensitive, side by side
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from SneppX_ALG import Tensor
from SneppX_ALG.interface_bindings import nn

pred = Tensor(np.array([0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 10.0], dtype=np.float32), requires_grad=True)
tgt = Tensor(np.zeros(4, dtype=np.float32))

mse = nn.MSELoss()(pred, tgt)
mse.backward()
print("MSE grad:", np.asarray(pred.grad.data))     # outlier at 10 dominates

Add an outlier to the target and MSELoss moves the whole batch; L1Loss or HuberLoss barely notice. That is the entire reason those losses exist.

import numpy as np
from SneppX_ALG import Tensor
from SneppX_ALG.interface_bindings import nn

pred = Tensor(np.zeros(4, dtype=np.float32), requires_grad=True)
tgt = Tensor(np.array([0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 10.0], dtype=np.float32))

for name, loss_fn in [("L1", nn.L1Loss()), ("Huber", nn.HuberLoss())]:
    loss = loss_fn(pred, tgt)
    loss.backward()
    print(name, "grad:", np.asarray(pred.grad.data))
    pred.zero_grad_()

docs.title: Classification losses
docs.text:
For a binary problem the logit z is mapped through a sigmoid. Plotting the loss against z shows why BCEWithLogitsLoss is numerically preferred over sigmoid followed by BCELoss: the fused form avoids log(0) when a prediction saturates.

import numpy as np
from SneppX_ALG import Tensor
from SneppX_ALG.interface_bindings import nn

logits = Tensor(np.array([-20.0, 0.0, 20.0], dtype=np.float32), requires_grad=True)
target = Tensor(np.array([1.0, 1.0, 1.0], dtype=np.float32))

loss = nn.BCEWithLogitsLoss()(logits, target)
loss.backward()
print("loss:", float(np.asarray(loss.data).reshape(-1)[0]))
print("grad:", np.asarray(logits.grad.data))   # saturates to 0 and -1, never NaN

See also: Optimizer race · Autograd visualizer · Cookbook.

docs.title: Matmul visualizer
docs.text:
Matrix multiplication is a sum of row · column dot products. Hover any cell of C to see exactly which row of A and which column of B produced it — and the arithmetic term by term.

A 3×4 × B 4×3 = C 3×3 🎲 Randomize ▶ Sweep all cells

docs.title: Why it matters for training
docs.text:
The same shape rule governs linear layers: an input (N, K) times a weight (K, N_out) produces (N, N_out). A shape mismatch like (N, C, L) @ (C,) fails instead of broadcasting — reshape the bias to (1, C, 1) first, as SNEPPX-Alg's Conv layers do.

import numpy as np
from SneppX_ALG import Tensor

x = Tensor(np.random.randn(2, 3).astype(np.float32))
w = Tensor(np.random.randn(3, 4).astype(np.float32))
print((x @ w).shape)          # (2, 4) — batch dimension preserved

docs.title: How matrix multiplication works
docs.text:
For A of shape (m, k) and B of shape (k, n), each output entry is a dot product:

C[i][j] = A[i][0]·B[0][j] + A[i][1]·B[1][j] + ... + A[i][k-1]·B[k-1][j]

Three rules follow from that formula:

  • Shape rule. The inner dimensions must match (k and k), and the result takes the outer dimensions: (m, k) @ (k, n) → (m, n).
  • Cost. Every one of the m·n outputs needs k multiply-adds, so a matmul costs m·n·k operations. This is why matmuls dominate the run time of Transformers and other dense networks.
  • Not commutative. A @ B and B @ A are generally different, and often only one of them has valid shapes.

In backpropagation, the gradients of C = A @ B are themselves matmuls: ∂L/∂A = ∂L/∂C @ Bᵀ and ∂L/∂B = Aᵀ @ ∂L/∂C.

See also: Autograd visualizer · Conv2d visualizer · Higher-order AD.

docs.title: Optimizer race
docs.text:
Four optimizers, same starting point, same loss surface. Press Start and watch SGD (momentum), Adam, AdamW, and NAdam race to the minimum.

surface elliptic bowl Rosenbrock curved valley ▶ Start Reset

docs.title: What to look for
docs.text:
• Elliptic bowl — high curvature in one direction. SGD with momentum zig-zags; Adam-family methods rescale per-coordinate and cut straight across.
  • Rosenbrock — the classic narrow curved valley. Momentum helps, but plain SGD needs far more steps; adaptive methods follow the valley quickly.
  • AdamW vs Adam — AdamW decouples weight decay, so it drifts slightly less.

These are illustrative dynamics (a plain JS implementation of the update rules), not a benchmark of the C engine. For the real implementations see optim.py and Cookbook → learning-rate warmup.

import numpy as np
from SneppX_ALG import Tensor
from SneppX_ALG.interface_bindings import nn, optim

for name, cls in [("SGD", optim.SGD), ("Adam", optim.Adam),
                  ("AdamW", optim.AdamW), ("NAdam", optim.NAdam)]:
    m = nn.Linear(4, 2)
    opt = cls(m.parameters(), lr=1e-2)
    x = Tensor(np.random.randn(8, 4).astype(np.float32))
    m(x).sum().backward()
    opt.step()
    opt.zero_grad()
    print(name, "ok")

docs.title: The update rules
docs.text:
With gradient g, learning rate lr and parameters θ, one step of each optimizer is:

SGD + momentum:  v = μ·v + g                    θ = θ − lr·v
Adam:            m = β1·m + (1−β1)·g            v = β2·v + (1−β2)·g²
                 θ = θ − lr · m̂ / (√v̂ + ε)      (m̂, v̂ are bias-corrected)
AdamW:           Adam step, then θ = θ − lr·λ·θ (decoupled weight decay)
NAdam:           Adam with a Nesterov look-ahead on the momentum term

Adam-family optimizers scale each parameter's step by its own gradient history, so they handle badly scaled loss surfaces better than plain SGD. SGD with momentum is simpler, uses less memory, and is still common for vision models.

See also: Autograd visualizer · Loss gallery.

docs.title: Post-Quantum Crypto Known-Answer Testing (PQC KAT) — status and write-up
docs.text: 2026-11-13 update. Companion to issue #16 (official NIST ACVP vector harness) in the SneppX/sneppx-alg tracker. The deterministic RNG used by seeded key-generation tests is now compiled only into explicit test builds.

docs.title: What was implemented
docs.text:
SneppX_ALG.interface_bindings.acvp_kat — a NIST ACVP harness for the C crypto backend (_SNEPPX_c.crypto), plus vendored official vectors: tests/data/acvp/*.json.

Test suites (availability depends on build configuration):

suite tests what it proves tests/python/test_acvp_sha3.py 4 C sha3_256 == NIST official KATs (40 byte-aligned SHA3-256 AFT vectors from SHA3-256-2.0), C==hashlib on the same messages, FIPS 202 empty-string KAT tests/python/test_acvp_mlkem.py conditional Deterministic keyGen and encaps/decaps tests require a test-only extension built with SNEPPX_ENABLE_TEST_RNG=ON; production builds skip this module. No FIPS validation is claimed. tests/python/test_acvp_slhdsa.py conditional Signature-verification vectors and C roundtrip/tamper tests; seeded determinism requires a test-only build. KeyGen vectors are explicitly skipped because they provide no reproducible entropy input accepted by the current C API. tests/python/test_acvp_mldsa.py conditional Signature-verification and roundtrip/tamper tests; deterministic keyGen vectors require a test-only extension built with SNEPPX_ENABLE_TEST_RNG=ON.

Vector provenance: usnistgov/ACVP-Server gen-val/json-files/ sample vector sets (NIST, public domain): SHA3-256-2.0, ML-KEM-keyGen-FIPS203, ML-KEM-encapsDecaps-FIPS203, ML-DSA-sigVer-FIPS204, ML-DSA-keyGen-FIPS204, SLH-DSA-sigVer-FIPS205, SLH-DSA-keyGen-FIPS205.

docs.title: Bit-level vector policy (why SHA3-256 subset is byte-aligned)
docs.text:
ACVP msg values are bit strings (len counts bits, final nibble zero-padded). The finalized SHA-3 approved function pads after the last message bit, so when len % 8 != 0 the digest is not the digest of any byte string: the padding pattern lands mid-byte. Those vectors equal the Keccak Team's ShortMsgKAT_SHA3-256.txt bit-level digests (verified against the published XKCP test-vector file).

Neither the C byte-string API nor Python hashlib can absorb bit-level messages, so we vendor byte-aligned (len % 8 == 0) vectors only for autonomous testing. ML-DSA/SLH-DSA sigVer messages are all byte-aligned (or have no msgLen), so their full sets are vendored.

Verifying bit-level KATs would require a bit-length sponge API on the C side; that is the documented follow-up.

docs.title: Honest interop report
docs.text:
acvp_kat.interop_report(crypto, vectors, runner) aggregates C-verifier decisions against NIST's testPassed flags.

  • SHA3-256: 100 % KAT agreement (C digest == NIST md == hashlib on all vendored vectors).
  • ML-KEM (Kyber): deterministic keygen and encaps/decaps KATs require the test-only RNG hook. That hook is not compiled into production builds. Keygen agreement is measured byte-for-byte against NIST ek/dk; the implementation remains experimental and is not FIPS validated.
  • ML-DSA & SLH-DSA: invalid foreign signatures are rejected, but valid finalized FIPS signatures are not fully interoperable with the current C wire formats. These implementations remain experimental.

Keygen coverage:

  • ML-KEM keyGen: run_mlkem_keygen() seeds the C test RNG with each vector's d value and compares ek/dk byte-for-byte against FIPS 203 expected values.
  • ML-DSA keyGen: run_mldsa_keygen() seeds the C test RNG with each vector's seed value and compares pk/sk against FIPS 204 expected values.
  • SLH-DSA keyGen: explicitly marked unsupported by the harness because the vendored sample set does not provide reproducible entropy inputs that can be passed to the current key-generation API. Those vectors are counted as skipped, not as successful interoperability.

The harness reports unsupported suites as skipped. It is a regression and interoperability tool, not a FIPS validation certificate. No invalid signature is accepted by the tested signature-verification paths.

docs.title: How to reproduce
docs.text:
$env:PYTHONPATH = "bindings/python"
python -m pytest tests/python/test_acvp_sha3.py -q -p no:cacheprovider
python -m pytest tests/python/test_acvp_mlkem.py -q -p no:cacheprovider
python -m pytest tests/python/test_acvp_slhdsa.py -q -p no:cacheprovider
python -m pytest tests/python/test_acvp_mldsa.py -q -p no:cacheprovider

The _SNEPPX_c extension must be built. Production builds omit deterministic RNG controls. To run seeded key-generation tests, configure a separate test build with -DSNEPPX_ENABLE_TEST_RNG=ON and build the Python extension. Never ship or distribute that test build. Signature-verification tests that do not need deterministic key generation can run against a production extension.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
SneppX-ALG organizes its security work into ten phases (S0-S9), covering cryptography, memory hardening, obfuscation, runtime monitoring, network security, AI sanitization, key management, secure updates, formal verification, and penetration-testing infrastructure. Implementation maturity varies by component: some areas are experimental, partial, or scaffolded. This document describes the intended architecture and current implementation evidence; it is not a security certification or a claim that every control is production-ready.

Each phase builds on the previous. The architecture is designed so that security is not a bolt-on layer but a property of the entire system.

For a time-stamped review of historical security and correctness findings, see the November 22, 2026 audit archive. That audit records findings at its audited commit and includes a remediation-commit ledger; its original counts are not a statement of current open vulnerabilities.

S0 ── S1 ── S2 ── S3 ── S4 ── S5 ── S6 ── S7 ── S8 ── S9
│     │     │     │     │     │     │     │     │     │
Crypto Memory Obfusc Monitor Network AI    UI    Update Formal Pentest
Core  Secure Engine  Engine  Sec   San    Sec   Sec    Verif  Report
      Mem

docs.title: S0 — Cryptographic Core (experimental)
docs.text:
Status: Experimental / partial Source: security/crypto/c/ and include/neural_core/security/

All crypto source files follow the four-layer commenting standard in COMMENTING.md: Layer 1 file headers, Layer 2 concept blocks, Layer 3 inline "why" comments, and Layer 4 Doxygen API docs on every public SNEPPX_* function.

docs.title: Primitives
docs.text:
Primitive Standard Use Case Verified Ed25519 RFC 8032 Signatures 304/306 test vectors pass X25519 RFC 7748 Key exchange Full DH exchange ChaCha20-Poly1305 RFC 8439 Authenticated encryption 100+ test vectors SHA-3 FIPS 202 Hashing (224/256/384/512) NIST test vectors SHA-256 FIPS 180-4 General-purpose hashing NIST test vectors BLAKE3 Reference Fast hashing Reference test vectors Argon2id RFC 9106 Secure KDF Test vectors + timing defense Secure Random OS CPRG Entropy Windows CNG / Linux getrandom Kyber-512/768/1024 Round-3 Kyber (ML-KEM lineage) PQ key encapsulation Experimental; not byte-compatible with FIPS 203; see report Dilithium-2/3/5 Round-3 Dilithium (ML-DSA lineage) PQ digital signatures Experimental; not byte-compatible with FIPS 204 SPHINCS+-128/192/256 Round-3 SPHINCS+ (SLH-DSA lineage) Stateless PQ signatures Experimental; not byte-compatible with FIPS 205

PQC validation limitations. The repository includes official NIST ACVP sample vectors and a harness, but this does not establish FIPS validation or full standards interoperability. SHA3-256 vectors match; ML-KEM checks include key-generation comparisons and encapsulation/decapsulation tests. The current ML-DSA and SLH-DSA C implementations reject invalid vectors but cannot yet verify all valid finalized FIPS signatures because their signature formats remain pre-finalization. See docs/pqc_kat.md for the detailed per-algorithm interop report. PQC remains experimental and should not be used as the sole protection for production secrets.

docs.title: API
docs.text:
#include "cryptographic_primitives_bundle.h"

// Ed25519 signing
uint8_t pk[32], sk[64];
SNEPPX_ed25519_keypair(pk, sk);
SNEPPX_ed25519_sign(sig, msg, msglen, sk, pk);

// ChaCha20-Poly1305 encryption
SNEPPX_chacha20_poly1305_encrypt(ct, &ctlen, pt, ptlen, key, nonce, aad, aadlen);

// Argon2id key derivation
SNEPPX_s0_argon2id_hash(hash, hashlen, pwd, pwdlen, salt, saltlen, t_cost, m_cost);

// Kyber key encapsulation (CCA-secure via Fujisaki-Okamoto transform)
SNEPPX_kyber_keypair(pk, sk, variant);
SNEPPX_kyber_encaps(ct, ss, pk, variant);
SNEPPX_kyber_decaps(ss, ct, sk, variant);

// Dilithium signatures
SNEPPX_dilithium_keypair(pk, sk, variant);
SNEPPX_dilithium_sign(sig, &siglen, msg, msglen, sk, variant);
SNEPPX_dilithium_verify(sig, siglen, msg, msglen, pk, variant);

// SPHINCS+ signatures (stateless, hash-based)
SNEPPX_sphincsplus_keypair(pk, sk, variant);
SNEPPX_sphincsplus_sign(sig, &siglen, msg, msglen, sk, variant);
SNEPPX_sphincsplus_verify(sig, siglen, msg, msglen, pk, variant);

docs.title: Known Issues
docs.text:
1. Ed25519 verification: historical documentation records 304/306 vectors passing. Re-run the current RFC 8032 vector suite and reconcile the remaining failures before claiming full compliance.
  2. Argon2 timing: historical tests reported timing variation on some hardware. Noise injection is not a substitute for constant-time design or side-channel analysis.
  3. PQ primitives: the ML-KEM checks are partial; ML-DSA and SLH-DSA valid-signature interoperability remains incomplete for finalized FIPS formats.

docs.title: Features
docs.text: Feature Description Guard Pages Allocate with PROT_NONE guard on both sides in debug mode Canaries Stack overflow detection on memory regions ASLR Heap randomization via VirtualAlloc (Windows) / mmap (Linux) Locked Memory mlock / VirtualLock to prevent swap to disk Secure Wipe Compiler-barrier-protected zeroing of sensitive data Constant-Time Compare Timing-attack-resistant memory comparison Memory Leak Detector Tracks allocations and reports unfreed blocks on shutdown

#include "protected_memory_manager.h"
#include "memory_leak_detector.h"

// Allocate locked memory (cannot be swapped to disk)
void* ptr = SNEPPX_s1_alloc_locked(4096);

// Securely free
SNEPPX_s1_free_locked(ptr, 4096);

// Constant-time comparison
int32_t match = SNEPPX_s1_memcmp_consttime(a, b, n);

// Memory leak detection
SNEPPX_memory_leak_detector_init(max_tracked_allocations);
void* p = malloc(256);
SNEPPX_memory_leak_detector_track(p, 256, "cache buffer");
SNEPPX_memory_leak_detector_untrack(p);
SNEPPX_memory_leak_detector_report(); // prints leaks to stderr

docs.title: S2 — Obfuscation Engine (known high-risk findings)
docs.text:
Current remediation: obfuscation_advanced.cpp no longer uses rand() / srand() for junk-pattern selection; it uses the S0 SNEPPX_random_bytes interface. The unsafe bogus control-flow rewrite APIs now fail closed and do not modify the supplied code buffer. This disables that feature rather than making it functional. Whitebox AES timing/alignment concerns and IAT concurrency findings remain open.

Status: Known high-risk findings remain open Source: security/obfuscation/ and security/cpp/

docs.title: Implemented
docs.text:
• Control flow flattening: converts natural control flow to switch-based dispatch
  • String encryption: XOR-based compile-time string obfuscation with rotating keys
  • Instruction substitution: replace ADD/SUB/MUL/AND/OR/XOR with NAND-gate equivalent sequences
  • Opaque predicates: always-true/false branches to confuse static analysis
  • Code virtualization: basic-block-level bytecode compilation with encrypted handler dispatch table
  • Anti-debug: ptrace detection, NtGlobalFlag check, timing anomaly detection, breakpoint scanning
  • Binary substitution: opcode-level replacement with prefix/suffix byte insertion
  • Junk code insertion: NOP slides, dead-store MOVs, identity XORs
  • Constant unfolding: integer constants expressed as (a + b) with random splits
  • IAT protection: hash-based import resolution, integrity scanning
  • SEH/VEH obfuscation: exception-based control flow
  • TLS callback obfuscation: runtime function pointer encoding
  • Anti-dump: PE/ELF header XOR encryption with CRC integrity verification
  • Multi-VM diversity: multiple bytecode handlers with slot switching
  • Instruction scheduling randomization: basic-block-level instruction reordering

docs.title: Explicitly disabled legacy scaffolding
docs.text:
• SNEPPX_bsdiff_with_signature() used XOR masking, not a digital signature; it now always fails closed.
  • SNEPPX_manifest_verify_from_buffer() compared a short non-cryptographic hash; it now always fails closed.
  • Legacy manifest creation and hashing also used weak, truncated non-cryptographic hashes; those APIs now fail closed without modifying output buffers.
  • These compatibility APIs do not authenticate updates. All legacy offline-bundle creation, signing, verification, and state-query APIs fail closed; a caller-supplied struct flag is not accepted as proof of a signature. Use the separate Ed25519-backed signed-update verifier only with a configured trusted public key and verified payload hashes.
  • TUF metadata/key-management APIs are compatibility stubs and now all fail closed. They do not generate, expose, revoke, sign, or verify trusted metadata.
  • TPM compatibility APIs now fail closed: PCR read/extend, quote, seal/unseal, and TPM-random calls return failure without modifying caller buffers. Legacy NV reads return UINT32_MAX; the void NV setter is a no-op. No TPM hardware-backed implementation is currently available.
  • A/B partition and bootloader APIs now fail closed. The previous implementation only changed in-memory state and fabricated slot hashes; it did not operate on partitions or a bootloader. No slot selection, rollback, or health result is reported as successful.
  • The legacy update-verifier private-key getter/setter now fail closed. The verifier stores only a trusted public key and never claims to retain or export a signing private key.
  • The legacy history-count setter rejects negative values and values beyond the fixed ten-entry history capacity.
  • Signed-update version and history state are process-local memory only. They are not persisted across restarts and are not a hardware-backed monotonic counter; deployments requiring durable anti-rollback must supply trusted persistent state.
  • Applying an already-current version is rejected to prevent same-version replay. Downgrade rejection still depends on the verifier's rollback-protection setting and its in-memory state.
  • The integrity-verification helper requires exactly a 32-byte Ed25519 public key and a 64-byte signature; truncated or trailing key/signature bytes are rejected.
  • Signed update bundles: Ed25519-signed update payloads with version rolling
  • Rollback rejection: process-local version/history checks; state is not durable across restarts or backed by a hardware monotonic counter
  • Staged rollout: gradual update distribution with health-check gating

docs.title: Threat Model
docs.text: The controls below are implementation areas, not guarantees that the corresponding threat is fully mitigated. Validation varies by component; see the known issues and phase status above.

docs.title: Assumptions
docs.text:
• The hardware is trusted (no side-channel attacks on CPU)
  • The OS is trusted (no kernel-level compromise)
  • The network is untrusted
  • Other AI models are untrusted and potentially adversarial
  • Supply-chain integrity must be verified by the deployment process; repository commits are not guaranteed to be signed

docs.title: Defenses
docs.text: Threat Defense area Status Signature forgery Ed25519 verification and trusted-key configuration Partial; caller and key-management paths require validation Data breach at rest ChaCha20-Poly1305 authenticated encryption Partial; backend availability and integration must be checked Side-channel timing Constant-time primitives Not fully verified; timing concerns remain Memory scraping Locked memory and guard pages Platform-dependent; independent validation required Swap forensics mlock / VirtualLock Platform-dependent; OS permissions and limits apply Reverse engineering Control-flow flattening and string obfuscation Partial Runtime tampering Behavioral monitor Partial Adversarial input ARC input guard Partial; not a complete policy boundary Gradient leakage ARC gradient obfuscation Experimental; efficacy not independently evaluated Model inversion ARC output verifier Experimental; not independently validated

docs.title: Reporting Vulnerabilities
docs.text: See SECURITY.md

docs.title: Security Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Always verify signatures: Use SNEPPX_ed25519_verify on any external data
  2. Lock sensitive data: Use SNEPPX_s1_alloc_locked for keys and secrets
  3. Wipe after use: Call SNEPPX_s1_free_locked or SNEPPX_secure_zero on sensitive buffers
  4. Use constant-time comparisons: Never use memcmp for secret comparison
  5. Use AEAD: Always use SNEPPX_chacha20_poly1305_encrypt with associated data
  6. Don't roll your own: Use the provided crypto primitives; do not implement your own

docs.title: S0 — Cryptographic Core
docs.text:
Purpose: Experimental cryptographic primitives for signing, encryption, hashing, and key exchange. Presence of an implementation does not establish production readiness, constant-time behavior, certification, or independent review.

Components:

  • Ed25519 (RFC 8032) signatures: historical documentation reports 304/306 vectors passing; current vector coverage must be reconciled before claiming full conformance
  • X25519 (RFC 7748) key exchange: Full DH exchange
  • ChaCha20-Poly1305 (RFC 8439) AEAD: encrypt/decrypt
  • SHA-3 (FIPS 202): 224/256/384/512
  • SHA-256 (FIPS 180-4): General-purpose hashing
  • BLAKE3: Fast hashing
  • Argon2id (RFC 9106): KDF implementation; historical timing tests reported platform-dependent variation
  • Secure Random: OS CPRNG (Windows CNG / Linux getrandom)
  • Kyber-512/768/1024 (round-3 Kyber; ML-KEM lineage): experimental PQ key encapsulation, not FIPS 203 byte-compatible
  • Dilithium-2/3/5 (round-3 Dilithium; ML-DSA lineage): experimental PQ signatures, not FIPS 204 byte-compatible
  • SPHINCS+-128/192/256 (round-3 SPHINCS+; SLH-DSA lineage): experimental PQ signatures, not FIPS 205 byte-compatible

Files: security/crypto/c/

PQC ACVP status: Official NIST ACVP sample vectors are vendored under tests/data/acvp/ and exercised through SneppX_ALG.interface_bindings.acvp_kat. Coverage is partial, not a claim of FIPS validation or certification: SHA3-256 vectors match; ML-KEM key-generation and encapsulation/decapsulation checks are present; ML-DSA and SLH-DSA currently reject invalid signature vectors but do not yet verify all valid finalized FIPS signatures because their C wire formats remain pre-finalization. See docs/pqc_kat.md for the interop report and limitations. Treat PQC support as experimental until those gaps are closed and independently reviewed.

docs.title: S1 — Memory Hardening
docs.text:
Purpose: Runtime memory protection against corruption, leakage, and exploitation.

Components:

  • Guard pages: Inaccessible pages placed before/after heap allocations
  • Stack canaries: Random values on stack, checked before function return
  • ASLR: Random base addresses for heap/mmap allocations
  • Locked memory: mlock() / VirtualLock to prevent swapping of secrets
  • Secure wipe: memset with compiler barrier (prevents optimizer removal)
  • Constant-time comparison: Timing-attack-resistant memcmp
  • Memory leak detector: Tracks allocations, reports unfreed blocks

Files: security/memory/
